lead: This unit covers how avionics are organised, shown to the crew and connected: platform needs, federated and integrated architectures, analog and glass cockpits, the PFD, MFD and head-up displays, the ARINC 429, MIL-STD-1553B and AFDX data buses, software assurance, and the transducers and electronics that turn a pressure or a temperature into a number. After it you can size a bus or a virtual link, read a display, and design a sensor chain from bridge to ADC code.
about: The unit runs from the whole aircraft down to one signal. It starts with what civil, military, space and unmanned platforms ask of their electronics and how avionics evolved, then shows how computers are arranged (federated boxes or shared IMA cabinets). Three chapters follow the cockpit from dials to glass screens, the standard display formats and head-up and helmet displays, with a short chapter on cockpit design. Two chapters cover the data buses that join everything, and a short chapter covers how flight software is assured. The last two chapters go to the signal itself: the transducers that measure pressure, temperature, strain, position and acceleration, and the diodes, transistors, op-amps, converters and microcontrollers that condition and digitise their outputs.

chapters.idea: Avionics is shaped by the platform: civil aircraft value safety and regularity, military aircraft value mission and survivability, spacecraft value autonomy and telemetry, UAVs value size, weight and remote control.
chapters.depth: Cover evolution from separate radios and instruments to integrated systems. Compare civil, military, spacecraft and UAV avionics by function, environment, redundancy and certification. Include ADS-B as a civil surveillance example and say details are in Unit 5. List payload types: radar, EO/IR, SIGINT, communications, stores and science packages; do not teach sensor physics. Mention organisation framework: sensors, processing, displays, data buses, power and cooling.

figure.aria: A taxonomy tree with Avionics at the root and four branches: Civil, Military, Spacecraft and UAV, each with two example functions.

chapters.example: Classify four functions: (a) ADS-B Out at 1090 MHz on a B737, (b) stores management on a fighter, (c) attitude control on a 3-axis satellite, (d) waypoint following on a 25 kg UAV. Answer: (a) civil, (b) military, (c) spacecraft, (d) UAV.
chapters.trap: Do not treat UAV avionics as small civil avionics; limited weight, power and datalink loss change the design.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 flight control basics help but are not required.
chapters.leave: ADS-B signal details, radar and ILS go to Unit 5; missile guidance goes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Architecture decides which boxes compute, which share resources, and how data reaches the cockpit.
chapters.depth: Define LRU: line replaceable unit, a box changed on the flight line. Compare federated architecture, where each LRU owns one function, with integrated modular avionics (IMA), where shared cabinets host software partitions. Cover IMA modules, backplanes, ARINC 653 partitioning (mention only), redundancy, BITE and maintenance data. Use organisation framework: sensors, computers, data buses, displays, power and cooling. Some syllabi call IMA 'integrated avionics'.

figure.title: Federated to IMA
figure.aria: Block diagram from sensors through federated LRUs to IMA modules, then AFDX to displays, with a maintenance branch.

chapters.example: A federated aircraft has 8 LRUs, each 2 kg and 40 W. An IMA cabinet replaces them with 3 modules, 5 kg total and 90 W. Find mass and power saved. Mass: 8×2=16 kg; saved 16−5=11 kg. Power: 8×40=320 W; saved 320−90=230 W.
chapters.trap: IMA saves weight and power but adds partitioning and certification work; do not claim it removes redundancy.
chapters.leave: Software partitioning detail to 4.9; electrical buses to Unit 3 and 4.7.

chapters.idea: The cockpit changed from many single-function analog dials to fewer glass displays fed by computers.
chapters.depth: Describe analog cockpit: direct-reading dials, mechanical linkages, dedicated warnings, high part count. Describe glass cockpit: CRT or LCD displays, symbol generators, reconfigurable pages, central warning. Cover hybrid cockpits with both. Mention different aircraft examples only as types, not named syllabi. Explain why glass improves information density but needs power, cooling and software assurance.

figure.title: Cockpit evolution
figure.aria: Four-stage block diagram from analog dials to hybrid, glass and integrated cockpits.

chapters.example: An analog cockpit has 24 dials. A glass cockpit replaces them with 4 displays, each showing 6 pages. How many pages in total, and how many dial functions per display if evenly split? Pages: 4×6=24. Functions per display: 24÷4=6.
chapters.trap: Glass cockpit does not mean paperless or sensorless; each display still needs valid sensor and symbol-generator data.
chapters.leave: Display symbol detail to 4.4; power and cooling to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Electronic displays turn aircraft state into standard screen formats: PFD for control, MFD for navigation and systems, with EADI and EHSI as older names.
chapters.depth: Define PFD: primary flight display, shows attitude, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, heading, flight director. MFD: multifunction display, selectable navigation, weather, engine or systems pages. EADI: electronic attitude director indicator, older name for attitude part; EHSI: electronic horizontal situation indicator, older name for navigation part. Cover EICAS and ECAM as engine and systems monitor displays; some syllabi call them electronic system monitor displays. Mention colour use, failure flags and reversion. Do not teach ILS components here.

figure.aria: Tree with Flight deck displays at the root and four children: PFD, MFD, EICAS and ECAM, with notes giving older names or roles.

chapters.example: A PFD screen is 200 mm × 150 mm. Attitude occupies 60% of its area. Find the attitude area. Screen area = 200×150 = 30,000 mm². Attitude area = 0.60×30,000 = 18,000 mm².
chapters.trap: EADI and EHSI are not two extra boxes on a glass aircraft; they are older display names now often merged into PFD and MFD.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3; Unit 3 air data and engine instruments.
chapters.leave: ILS to Unit 5; display hardware electronics to 4.11.

chapters.idea: HUD and HMD keep flight and mission symbols in the pilot's line of sight so the eyes need not look down.
chapters.depth: Explain HUD: symbol generator, projector, collimating optics, combiner glass, pilot eye. Symbols focus at infinity. Cover HMD: helmet-mounted display, head tracker, monocular or binocular, used for cueing and night vision. Mention military vs civil HUD use. Keep safety and ergonomics brief; detail is in 4.6.

figure.title: HUD and HMD light path
figure.aria: Block diagram from symbol generator and projector to combiner and pilot eye, with a helmet display branch.

chapters.example: A HUD combiner is 75 mm above the pilot's eye and 500 mm forward. Find the look-down angle θ. tan θ = 75/500 = 0.150; θ = arctan 0.150 ≈ 8.5°.
chapters.trap: HUD symbols are collimated to infinity; they are not just a small screen pasted on glass.
chapters.leave: Human factors detail to 4.6; optics theory out of scope.

chapters.idea: Cockpit design matches displays, controls and warnings to human limits so the crew can fly and manage systems safely.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover human-machine interface (HMI), information hierarchy, colour and alert conventions, master caution and warning, control placement, workload, automation mode awareness, error and fatigue. Mention FAR/CS 25.1302 style usability ideas without naming syllabi. Keep shorter; focus on vocabulary and one design checklist.

figure.aria: Stack of five cockpit HMI layers from pilot at the top to automation at the bottom, showing displays, controls and warnings between them.

chapters.example: A pilot scans 6 displays with 0.4 s dwell per display. Find one full scan time. If a warning must be seen within 2 s, is one scan enough? Scan = 6×0.4 = 2.4 s, so one full scan is not enough; warning must be separate and salient.
chapters.trap: More information on screen is not better HMI; clutter and mode confusion are failures.
chapters.leave: Display hardware to 4.4; autopilot modes to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Data buses replace point-to-point wires with defined words, timing and error checks.
chapters.depth: ARINC 429: one-way, two-wire, 32-bit word, 12.5 or 100 kbps, label, SDI, data, SSM, parity; used for civil LRUs. MIL-STD-1553B: bidirectional command/response, 1 Mbps, Manchester II, 20-bit words (16 data), bus controller and remote terminals, dual redundant. Mention ARINC 429 high/low speed and 1553 word types. Compare topology, direction and use.

figure.aria: Sequence diagram of MIL-STD-1553B command, status and data words between bus controller and remote terminal.

chapters.example: Find one word time for ARINC 429 at 100 kbps with a 32-bit word, and for MIL-STD-1553B at 1 Mbps with a 20-bit word. ARINC: 32/100,000 = 0.32 ms. 1553: 20/1,000,000 = 0.02 ms = 20 µs. A 1553 message with command, data and status words takes 3×20 = 60 µs ignoring gaps.
chapters.trap: ARINC 429 is one-way; a reply needs another 429 channel. 1553B is command/response, not a free-running broadcast.

chapters.idea: AFDX gives switched Ethernet with guaranteed virtual links; fibre gives high bandwidth and immunity to electrical interference.
chapters.depth: AFDX: ARINC 664 part 7, 100 Mbps switched Ethernet, end systems, switches, virtual links, bandwidth allocation gap (BAG), redundancy management, frame integrity. Explain VL as a logical path with reserved bandwidth. Fibre-optic communication: light source, fibre, detector; multimode vs single-mode only briefly; advantages: high bandwidth, low weight, EMI immunity; disadvantages: connectors, bending, cost. Keep maths simple.

figure.title: AFDX switched network
figure.aria: Block diagram of AFDX end systems and switches, with a virtual link reserving bandwidth.

chapters.example: An AFDX virtual link has BAG 2 ms and maximum frame 1000 bytes. Find the reserved bandwidth. 1000 bytes = 8000 bits. Rate = 8000/0.002 = 4,000,000 bit/s = 4 Mbps.
chapters.trap: AFDX is not plain Ethernet; virtual links and BAG give bounded latency. Fibre does not remove the need for redundancy.
chapters.leave: Protocol software to 4.9; EMI/EMC packaging to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: DO-178B ties software assurance to failure consequence; the V-model makes requirements, design, code and tests traceable.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cover RTCA DO-178B as guidance for airborne software, not law. Software levels A to E from catastrophic to no safety effect. Objectives, planning, requirements, design, code, verification, configuration management, quality assurance. V-model: left side decomposition, right side verification; traceability both ways. Mention MC/DC for level A briefly. Keep shorter.

figure.title: DO-178B V-model
figure.aria: Flow from aircraft requirements down to code, then up through unit, integration and validation tests.

chapters.example: A function's failure is catastrophic, so it is level A. It has 40 requirements; 38 have traced tests. Find traceability. 38/40 = 0.95 = 95%. The two gaps must be closed before certification.
chapters.trap: DO-178B does not prescribe a programming language or a development tool; it asks for evidence that objectives are met.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 IMA partitioning; basic software testing helps.
chapters.leave: Hardware certification and ARINC 653 detail out of scope.

chapters.idea: Transducers convert physical quantities to electrical signals; avionics uses them for actuation, pressure, temperature, strain, position and acceleration.
chapters.depth: Define transducer and sensor. Solenoid: electromagnetic actuator, on/off or proportional. Pressure: bourdon tube, diaphragm, strain-gauge pressure transducer. Temperature: RTD, thermocouple, thermistor. Strain: strain gauge with gauge factor and bridge. Rotary position: potentiometer, LVDT, resolver, RVDT. Accelerometer: piezoelectric or MEMS; range, sensitivity, axis. Include signal form and typical aircraft use. Keep circuit detail to 4.11.

figure.aria: Taxonomy tree with Transducers at the root and six branches for solenoid, pressure, temperature, strain, position and acceleration, each with one example.

chapters.example: A 350 Ω strain gauge has gauge factor 2 and is strained by 500 µε. Find ΔR. ΔR/R = GF×ε = 2×500×10⁻⁶ = 0.001. ΔR = 0.001×350 = 0.35 Ω.
chapters.trap: A thermocouple measures temperature difference, not absolute temperature, unless cold-junction compensation is added.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.11 for signal conditioning; Unit 3 engine instruments.
chapters.leave: ADC and amplifier design to 4.11; gyroscopes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Avionics electronics turns small sensor signals into clean digital values and drives actuators under microcontroller control.
chapters.depth: Cover diode: one-way valve, rectifier, flyback protection. Transistor: switch and amplifier; MOSFET for power. Op-amp: ideal rules, inverting and non-inverting gain, buffer, differential amplifier for bridges. Signal conditioning: amplification, filtering, isolation, linearisation. ADC: resolution, sampling, quantisation; DAC: output drive. Microcontroller: CPU, memory, I/O, timers, serial ports; used for control and monitoring. Keep formulas and one signal chain.

figure.title: Signal chain
figure.aria: Block diagram of a sensor signal chain from bridge and amplifier through filter, ADC, microcontroller, DAC and actuator.

chapters.example: An 8-bit ADC has reference 5 V. Find resolution and the code for 1.000 V. Resolution = 5/2⁸ = 5/256 = 0.01953 V = 19.5 mV. Code = floor(1.000/0.01953) = 51.
chapters.trap: An 8-bit ADC has 256 codes but 255 steps; do not use 255 for resolution when the full-scale range is Vref.
chapters.leave: Power electronics and aircraft electrical distribution to Unit 3; software process to 4.9.
